speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me exactly which antibiotic you were taking, and how long ago did you start the rash and joint pain after beginning the medication?

speaker: Patient
text: 8-year-old girl. The patient was brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of low-grade fever, itchy rash, and generalized joint pain. The rash initially started in the antecubital and popliteal fossae before spreading to the trunk and distal extremities. One week ago, she was diagnosed with acute sinusitis and started on amoxicillin. She has no history of adverse drug reactions, and her immunizations are up to date.

speaker: Doctor
text: Did the symptoms resolve when you stopped the amoxicillin, and have they returned if you were re-exposed to it? I need to know if there is any swelling of the face, lips, or difficulty breathing, or if the rash is painful rather than just itchy.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the patient have any swollen lymph nodes, sore throat, or dark urine, and has she had any recent exposure to ticks or other patients with similar symptoms? I need to rule out serum sickness-like reaction versus an infectious etiology like Lyme disease or viral exanthem.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Diagnosed with acute sinusitis one week ago, no known history of adverse drug reactions, immunizations up to date. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the patient have any swollen lymph nodes, and is there any swelling of the hands or feet? I also need to know if the rash is raised and wheal-like or more like small red spots, and whether the joint pain is accompanied by visible swelling.

speaker: Doctor
text:
REQUEST TEST: Complete_Blood_Count, Comprehensive_Metabolic_Panel, Urinalysis
REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Urinalysis: Appearance Normal, WBC Within normal limits, RBC Within normal limits, Protein Negative, Glucose Negative. Complete_Blood_Count: NORMAL READINGS. Comprehensive_Metabolic_Panel: NORMAL READINGS.

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal labs and lack of systemic involvement strongly suggest a serum sickness-like reaction rather than true serum sickness or an infectious cause. DIAGNOSIS READY: Serum sickness-like reaction
